"You're going to the ward meeting again? It's Sunday, Rehana."
"It's about the old library building, Gopika. They want to turn it into a parking lot."
"And what will one meeting do?"
"Last time only six people came. If sixty come, the councillor has to listen." Rehana tied her dupatta and picked up a folder. "I've got photos of the carved doors, and the list of manuscripts Dada helped catalogue."
"You're not even an architect."
"No, but I teach the kids' reading hour there. Where will they go?"
Gopika sighed and reached for her own shoes. "Fine. I'm coming. But if it's boring, you're buying me chai."
"Deal. And bring your neighbour's son. He's fourteen. He should see how these decisions get made."
"You want to drag a teenager to a civic meeting?"
"I want him to know he's allowed to be in the room."

qa.q: What does the council want to turn the old library building into?
qa.a: They want to turn it into a parking lot.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel about bringing the fourteen-year-old to the meeting?
qa.a: She feels hopeful and determined, wanting him to know he is allowed to be in the room when civic decisions get made.

qa.q: What could Rehana do to bring more people like Gopika along next time?
qa.a: She could share the photos and the kids' reading hour story ahead of time, so people see exactly what is at stake before the meeting.

qa.q: How does Gopika's view of the meeting change during the scene?
qa.a: She starts doubtful that one meeting can do anything, but Rehana's reasons about the kids and the numbers win her over enough to put on her shoes.

grounding: It shows civic stewardship: joining local governance to preserve a heritage building and guiding the next generation.

passage: When I started the heritage walks, I thought it was just a hobby. I'd grown up in these lanes and knew every temple bell and every old haveli door. One Saturday I brought nine schoolkids, and one of them, Sahil, asked, "Kunal bhaiya, why are the carvings on this wall half broken?" I didn't know. That bothered me. So I spent two weeks in the city archive and at the municipal office, reading dull files and asking polite questions. It turned out a road widening had cut the building in half. I went back and told Sahil's group the whole story, then we wrote a short letter to the ward office asking for a plaque. It took four months, but the plaque went up. Sahil's now fourteen and he leads the first stretch of the walk himself. I just follow and fill in dates.

qa.q: How many schoolkids came on the Saturday walk when Sahil asked his question?
qa.a: Nine schoolkids came.

qa.q: Why did it bother Kunal that he couldn't answer Sahil's question?
qa.a: He felt responsible and uneasy about not knowing, since he cared about the lanes' history and the kids learning it properly.

qa.q: Which choice by Kunal worked best, and why?
qa.a: He researched the real answer and then involved the kids in writing to the ward office, which turned curiosity into a small, lasting civic result.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sahil to now lead part of the walk?
qa.a: He probably feels trusted and proud, knowing that a question he asked as a child became a plaque and a role he now holds. 😊

grounding: It illustrates preserving cultural legacy through the proper civic channels and passing it on to the next generation.

Project note, District Library Oral History Project. Written by Neelam, coordinator.
Amandeep, 24, joined us in March as a volunteer. Within weeks he had recorded eleven elders from the old weaving colony, including two who had never been interviewed before. What stood out was his patience: he sat through long pauses, asked permission before every recording, and returned each transcript to the family for corrections. In June he offered to train a group of college students. He did not lecture them; he paired each student with one elder and stayed in the corner, stepping in only when a student interrupted too much. He also filed our request with the municipal archive properly, forms and all, so the recordings will be kept on public record. Next step: I have asked him to write a short guide for new volunteers, and to lead the next training himself.

qa.q: How many elders had Amandeep recorded within weeks?
qa.a: He had recorded eleven elders from the old weaving colony.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's habit of returning transcripts to families suggest about what he cares about?
qa.a: It suggests he respects the elders' ownership of their stories and wants the record to be accurate, not just collected.

qa.q: How could Neelam support Amandeep as he takes on more leadership?
qa.a: Neelam could give him time to write the guide, check in after his first solo training, and keep backing his careful methods.

qa.q: How might one of the elders see this project?
qa.a: An elder who had never been interviewed might feel honoured that their memories are being kept and checked with their family.

grounding: It shows civic stewardship of cultural heritage and mentoring the next generation, through a coordinator's note.

passage:
14 November

Long day but a good one. Our heritage walk group finally got permission to clean the old stepwell behind the tehsil office. Twenty of us turned up at seven with gloves and sacks. Vaibhav brought his students from the government school, and I spent an hour showing them the carvings: the elephants, the woman carrying water pots. One boy asked, "Didi, who made this?" I said, "People from this town, three hundred years ago. And now it's your job to look after it." He looked at the stone like it belonged to him. That was my favourite moment.

In the afternoon I helped at the voter registration camp near the market. Only eleven people came, which was disappointing.

I'm tired, but I feel like I spent today on something that will last. Next month: the kids make a guidebook.

— Gargi

qa.q: How many people came to the voter registration camp?
qa.a: Only eleven people came to the camp near the market.

qa.q: What does Gargi mean when she says she spent the day on something that will last?
qa.a: She feels her effort matters beyond today, because caring for the stepwell and teaching children passes the town's heritage and civic habits forward.

qa.q: How could Gargi get more people to the next registration camp?
qa.a: She could ask the students or local shopkeepers to spread the word, or hold it alongside a heritage event people already enjoy.

qa.q: How might the boy who asked who made the stepwell see the town now?
qa.a: He seems to feel the heritage belongs to him, which may make him more likely to protect it as he grows up.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young woman preserving local heritage, supporting civic processes and guiding the next generation.

Jomon: you've been doing this every weekend since march man. and the ward meeting stuff
Uday: someone has to show up to the ward meetings 😅 otherwise only 3 people decide everything
Jomon: true
Uday: I just don't want these songs to die with that generation
Jomon: they won't now 🙂

qa.q: Who will sing the old boat songs on Sunday?

qa.q: What is Uday worried about, and what drives Uday's effort?

qa.q: Which part of Uday's plan helps the songs survive longest?

qa.q: How might the grandmothers feel about being recorded?
